bib.title: GLTR: Statistical Detection and Visualization of Generated Text
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 57th Annual Meeting of the ACL: System Demonstrations (Florence, Italy)

question: Can simple statistical tests under a language model, shown as a visual overlay, help non-experts detect machine-generated text?
hypothesis: Generation systems over-sample from the head of the distribution, so generated text uses fewer low-rank words than human text; this should hold in black-box settings when a different large LM is used for detection.
contributions: Three simple statistical tests (word probability, word rank, predictive entropy) for detecting generated text
GLTR, an open-source, publicly deployed visual tool built on these tests
A human-subjects study showing the overlay improves human detection of fake text

method.summary: Per-token probability, rank and entropy are computed under a detection LM (GPT-2 117M or BERT) and rendered as a colour overlay (top-10 green, top-100 yellow, top-1,000 red, rest purple) plus histograms. Features were validated with logistic regression on 3 generated and 3 human sources, and with a 35-student study with and without the overlay.

eval.protocol: Cross-validation: train on each combination of four of the six sources (two real/fake), test on remaining two. Human study: 35 volunteer students in a college-level NLP class, two rounds of 5 texts (no overlay, then overlay with a brief tutorial between), each round 2 GPT-2 (temp 0.7), 1 Heliograf, 2 NYT, texts randomly assigned to rounds across students; treatment effect controlled for native-speaker status and rated difficulty.

limits: Authors concede the core assumption is biased (head-of-distribution) sampling; adversarial schemes could fool the overlay, though sampling from the tail reduces coherence.
Samples conditioned on a hidden seed text have a different conditional distribution; only preliminary qualitative investigation of this.
Small data: 50 articles per source, six sources, high AUC variance (+-0.07 to +-0.27); human study uses 35 students from one NLP class, 5 texts per round; no false-positive-rate analysis.

Detector models are 2019-era (GPT-2 117M, BERT); modern LLMs with different sampling and instruction tuning are untested. Related work notes entropy findings reversed vs Lavergne et al. 2008 as LMs improved.
Does not detect misinformation content; only statistical signature.
